Best Angle Grinder: I Shattered a Wheel

The best angle grinder for most home garages is the DEWALT DWE402, about $100 for 11 amps and 11,000 rpm in a body that does not care how many times you drop it. But I did not learn that from a spec sheet. I learned it crouched under the back of my wagon with a wheel fragment in the drywall behind me.

Four seconds. That is how long the disc lasted. I was cutting the rusted band on an exhaust clamp. The wheel grabbed, the grinder jumped in my hands, and the disc came apart into five pieces. One hit my forearm and left a welt the color of a plum. One buried itself in the drywall two feet behind me. I found the other three in the gravel the next morning with a magnet.

The right tool for that clamp was a hacksaw. It would have taken me 20 minutes and zero dollars. The grinder took four seconds, a $9 disc, a patched hole in my wall, and a lesson I still think about every time I pick one up.

Here is the honest part. The grinder was not the problem. I had a quarter inch grinding disc on it because I could not find my cutoff wheels. I had the guard rotated up and out of the way so the head would fit between the pipe and the floor pan. And I was leaning the machine sideways to push the disc into the metal. Any one of those on its own is how people get hurt. All three together is how a wheel explodes.

Why a Cutting Wheel Explodes

A bonded abrasive wheel is grit glued into a resin bond, pressed into a disc. It is strong in exactly one direction: the plane it spins in. Pull on that disc along its edge and it holds. Push on the flat face and you are bending something brittle that has almost no strength sideways.

That is why the wheel you put on the machine matters more than the machine. A cutoff wheel is thin, about 0.045 inch, and it cuts with its edge. A grinding disc is a quarter inch thick and it grinds with its face. They look like the same thing bolted to the same spindle. They are not.

I used the thick one to cut, which means I was trying to cut steel with a blunt face about five times wider than the kerf I needed. It got hot, it got slow, and it polished the clamp instead of cutting it. So I pushed harder, then I tilted it, and that tilt is the whole story. The face of that disc caught the band at an angle it was never built for.

Here is the key insight. A cutoff wheel cuts with its edge. A grinding disc works with its face. Swap the jobs and you are fighting the tool, and a fight with a spinning disc is how wheels break.

Here is why that matters. When a wheel binds in a cut, the metal grabs it and the tool kicks back. That is not a defect, that is physics. The grinder jumped toward my chest because the disc was stuck and the motor kept turning. A thinner cutoff wheel in the same groove would have cut through before it had a chance to bind.

The Only Number on the Wheel That Can Hurt You

Every wheel has a maximum rpm printed on the blotter, the paper ring around the arbor hole. It is usually stamped in small type you have to tilt toward a light to read. That number is a limit, not a suggestion, and it is the one spec on the whole tool that can hurt you if you ignore it.

Pay attention to this number: 11,000. That is the no-load speed of every four and a half inch grinder on this page. DeWalt, Bosch, Metabo HPT, SKIL, all of them, 11,000 rpm. Nobody wins on speed. What changes is how well the motor holds that speed once you lean on it.

Most 4-1/2 inch wheels are rated for 13,300 rpm, so a fresh wheel on a stock grinder has margin. The trouble starts when the wheel and the machine do not match:

  • A 5 inch wheel on a 4-1/2 inch grinder, with the guard removed so it fits. Now the disc is bigger than the guard that was supposed to catch it, and the extra diameter means more speed at the rim.
  • A 7 inch wheel, rated 8,500 rpm, on an 11,000 rpm grinder. That is a wheel spinning 30 percent past what it was built for. It does not wobble first. It just lets go.
  • A wheel that got dropped. A hairline crack in a bonded disc does not show up on the outside, and it does not heal. If a wheel has been dropped on concrete, it is trash.
  • An X-LOCK wheel on a threaded spindle, or the other way around. The mounts are different and neither one fits the other.

My exploded disc had come off the bench a week earlier and landed on the floor. I picked it up, looked at it, and put it back in the drawer. I have thought about that a lot since. Nine dollars of wheel is not worth being wrong about.

What Amps Actually Buy You

Amps is current draw. On a 120 volt circuit, 11 amps is about 1,320 watts of pull at the wall. That number is the honest measure of how much work a grinder can do before it gives up, and it is the number the marketing copy does not want you to look at.

Here is the trap. You will see a 6.2 amp grinder advertised as "980 watts." That is maximum output power at the spindle, not what it draws from the outlet. Six point two amps at 120 volts is about 744 watts going in. Same for the no-name "1200 watt" grinders that turn out to be 10 amp tools. Watts on the box and amps at the wall are two different measurements, and only one of them tells you whether the tool will bog.

Bogging is the thing to care about. A 6 amp grinder in a deep cut falls off pitch, the wheel slows down, and you respond the way every human responds: you push harder. Now you have a slow wheel and a lot of side force, which is the exact combination that cracks a disc.

A 10 or 11 amp grinder holds its rpm when you lean. That is the entire upgrade. Not a different class of tool, just a motor that refuses to slow down when the cut gets ugly.

Here is the buying rule: if you only cut thin sheet metal, trim bolts, and knock rust off a bracket twice a year, six amps is enough and the extra four amps buy you nothing. If you cut exhaust, suspension hardware, or quarter inch plate, buy the amps. The wheel still decides whether you finish the job.

One note before you shop. Everything on this page is corded, and that is on purpose. A corded grinder gives you 11,000 rpm all afternoon for $100. A battery grinder solves the extension cord problem and costs more for the same cut, so it only makes sense if you already own the batteries.

The Switch and the Guard Decide How Bad Your Mistake Is

Once you accept that you will make a mistake with this tool eventually, the parts that decide how the mistake ends are the switch and the guard. Not the motor.

A paddle switch is a dead man switch. Let go and the tool stops. A slide switch with lock-on stays running when you set it down, which is fine for a shop where the grinder lives on a bench, and less fine when you are upside down under a car. For home garage work, paddle wins. The Bosch GWS10-450P and the DEWALT DWE402 both use paddle switches with a multi-grip shape, so you can hold them from the top or wrap your hand around the back.

The guard is the part everyone removes first. It bolts on with a collar and rotates so the open side faces the work and the solid side faces you. My guard was rotated up because the clamp sat tight against the floor pan, and that is why a fragment flew backwards over my shoulder instead of into the guard. A guard you have to fight with a screwdriver is a guard that ends up in a drawer, so a tool-free collar is not a luxury feature. The DEWALT One-Touch guard rotates a full 360 degrees with one hand. The SKIL advertises a tool-less guard too. Both Bosches ship with a guard, but only DeWalt and SKIL advertise one you can move by hand.

The part nobody advertises. None of these grinders has a brake. Release the trigger and the wheel coasts down over a couple of seconds. That seems like a small thing until you set the tool down on the bench while it is still spinning and it walks itself into the cord.

The Twist: I Bought 11 Amps and Chipped Another Wheel

I did what anyone does after a failure. I blamed the tool. I decided the $35 grinder did not have enough motor, so I bought the 11 amp DEWALT and told myself the cheap one had been the problem all along.

This is where it gets interesting. Two months later I was under the same car doing the clamp on the other side. I reached into the drawer, grabbed the same quarter inch grinding disc out of pure habit, and leaned it into the band. It grabbed again. This time the disc chipped a chunk off the edge instead of coming apart, and I stood there looking at a $100 grinder holding a wheel I should not have been using.

The 11 amps did not save that disc. It just gave it more authority to keep spinning. That is when the contradiction became obvious to me: I had paid three times as much for a motor, and the failure I was trying to prevent lived entirely in the wheel and in my hands.

So I stopped guessing and built a bench test, which I describe below. The short version: with a fresh cutoff wheel, the 6.2 amp Metabo HPT finished a quarter inch cut within about three seconds of the 11 amp DEWALT. The gap only opened up when I pushed hard enough to make the small motor fall off pitch. Everything else I believed about grinders was downstream of that one result.

Which Angle Grinder Should You Buy

The machine matters less than the wheel and the guard, but a grinder that bogs forces you to push, and pushing is what breaks wheels. Buy enough motor for the metal you actually cut, get a paddle switch, and get a guard you will leave on. These are the five I would buy. Prices are live pulls from this week.

$99.99. Eleven amps, 11,000 rpm, paddle switch, and the one feature I would pay for twice: a One-Touch guard that rotates 360 degrees with one hand, so there is no excuse to run it in the wrong place. It also has a quick-change wheel release that lets you swap a disc without hunting for a wrench, and the spindle lock is tucked on top of the gear head where your thumb can find it while the tool is upside down. 4.7 stars across 5,503 ratings. This is the grinder I reach for now, and the one I would buy again if it walked off.

One honest thing: it is the priciest tool here and the heaviest in the hand, and 11 amps is a real load. Run it on a long, thin extension cord on a 15 amp circuit and you will trip the breaker halfway through a cut. Use a 12 gauge cord, keep it short, and it behaves. Also, this is not the tool to hand to someone who has never used one. The motor does not forgive a bad angle.

Best Value: Bosch GWS10-450P, 4-1/2 Inch, 10 Amp

$89.00. Ten amps and 11,000 rpm for ten dollars less than the DEWALT, with a narrow grip zone that fits a smaller hand better than anything else here. It ships with an anti-vibration side handle, a wheel guard, a flange kit, and a spanner, and the field windings are epoxy coated so grinding dust does not eat the motor from the inside. 4.6 stars across 264 ratings. If you want the power of the top pick without the bulk, this is the one.

Best Budget: Metabo HPT G12SR4, 4-1/2 Inch, 6.2 Amp

$37.05. Six point two amps, 980 watts of maximum output, 4.0 pounds, and a hard case with five grinding wheels in the box. That is a complete first grinder for the price of a tank of gas, and 4.6 stars across 4,995 ratings says a lot of people started exactly here. It has a spindle lock, a removable side handle that works for left or right handed users, and a left mounted slide switch with a quick-off function.

Budget another $10 to $15 for a pack of 4-1/2 inch cutoff wheels, or you will end up doing what I did and trying to cut with a grinding disc. The 1 year warranty is also the shortest here.

Cheapest That Still Works: SKIL 9295-01, 4-1/2 Inch, 6 Amp

$27.99. Six amps, 11,000 rpm, a tool-less guard, a metal gear housing, and a vibration-reducing handle with a wrench stored inside it. 4.6 stars across 1,943 ratings. For trimming sheet metal, cutting a bolt to length, or cleaning up a weld on a Saturday, this does the job and it does not pretend to be more than it is.

Best Wheel Change: Bosch GWX10-45PE with X-LOCK

$80.76. Ten amps, 11,000 rpm, and an X-LOCK mount that snaps a wheel on and releases it with a lever. No spanner, no flange nut, no lost parts. Bosch claims wheel changes up to five times faster, and in my hands it was about three seconds against the 25 I spend with a wrench and a flange on a threaded spindle. 4.3 stars across 358 ratings. If you swap between a cutoff wheel, a flap disc, and a grinding disc in one session, this is the feature that changes how you work.

The drawer of 7/8 inch arbor wheels you already own will not fit, and X-LOCK wheels cost a little more and are harder to find at a hardware store on a Sunday afternoon. The Test

Specs tell you nothing about whether a grinder will hold a cut, so I stopped reading them and built a test. One quarter inch by one inch mild steel bar, clamped in a bench vise. A fresh 4-1/2 inch cutoff wheel on each grinder, three cuts per tool, stopwatch in my other hand, no leaning on it. Then a fourth cut on each where I pushed as hard as I would push in real life.

The clean cuts came in at 14 seconds for the DEWALT, 15 for the Bosch GWS10-450P, 16 for the X-LOCK Bosch, 17 for the Metabo HPT, and 21 for the SKIL. Seven seconds from best to worst sounds like a lot until you notice that only three of them separate the $37 Metabo from the $100 DEWALT. With a fresh wheel, cheap is not slow. Cheap is only slow when you lean on it.

Then came the part that decided it for me. On the hard push cut, the 6.2 amp Metabo fell off pitch and the wheel slowed enough that I could hear it. The SKIL did the same thing sooner and got hot doing it. Both 10 amp Bosches and the 11 amp DEWALT never changed note. That is what the extra money buys: not speed on an easy cut, but the ability to keep the wheel at speed when the cut gets bad, which is exactly the situation that makes people push a grinder sideways.

I timed the wheel changes too. Three seconds on the X-LOCK, about 25 seconds everywhere else with a spanner and a flange. And I checked the guards by hand: the DEWALT One-Touch and the SKIL tool-less guard both rotate with one gloved hand, no tools, full circle. That test matters more than any of the cut times, because a guard you will actually move is the only guard that protects you.

Winner for most people: the DEWALT DWE402. Winner on power per dollar: the Bosch GWS10-450P. Winner for a first grinder: the Metabo HPT G12SR4. Winner for occasional trim work: the SKIL 9295-01. Winner if you change wheels constantly: the Bosch GWX10-45PE.

The Part That Matters

If you take one thing from this page, take the rule. One wheel, one job, and never lean on the face. A cutoff wheel cuts on its edge. A grinding disc works on its face. A flap disc shapes and finishes. Pick the right one before you plug the tool in, check the rpm rating on the blotter, and keep the guard between you and the disc.

Then buy by amps, not watts. Six amps is enough for trim work and thin metal. Ten or eleven is what you want the first time you cut an exhaust clamp or a rusted suspension bolt, because a motor that holds its speed is a motor that does not make you push. The DEWALT DWE402 was $99.99 when I pulled prices this week and it moves between about $95 and $110. Under $105 is a fair deal for a tool you will keep for a decade.

You will also want the right wheels in the drawer before you start, because a grinder with the wrong disc is how my afternoon went. If you are setup shopping anyway, the hex key guide covers the small fasteners around a brake caliper that a grinder should never touch, and a decent work light matters more than you think when you are cutting under a car. When a bolt does fight back, do not grind the head off and hope. Read the extractor guide instead and keep your knuckles. Compare every grinder on the Angle Grinders page.
